notes:
1. Reservation — Meaning

  • Reservation is a form of affirmative action through which specified opportunities are set apart for groups that have historically faced exclusion, discrimination or inadequate representation.
  • It seeks substantive equality rather than merely identical treatment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Historical Exclusion → Affirmative Action → Representation → Equality of Opportunity

2. Major Areas of Reservation

Reservation operates principally in:

  • Educational admissions.
  • Public employment.
  • Promotions in specified circumstances.
  • Legislative representation.
  • Local-government representation.

3. Reservation Is Not Merely an Anti-Poverty Programme

Traditional caste-based reservation primarily addresses:

  • Historical discrimination.
  • Social and educational backwardness.
  • Institutional exclusion.
  • Inadequate representation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Social Backwardness ≠ Economic Poverty Alone

4. Formal Equality vs Substantive Equality

  • Formal equality means treating similarly situated persons alike.
  • Substantive equality recognises that historically disadvantaged groups may require corrective measures to achieve meaningful equality.
📌 Must-Memorise

Reservation → Instrument of Substantive Equality

5. Article 14

  • Article 14 guarantees:
  • Equality before law.
  • Equal protection of laws.
  • Equality does not always require identical treatment where circumstances differ substantially.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 14 → Equality Before Law + Equal Protection

6. Article 15

  • Article 15 prohibits discrimination on specified grounds including religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth.
  • It also contains clauses permitting constitutionally authorised affirmative action.

7. Article 15(3)

  • Article 15(3) permits special provisions for:
  • Women.
  • Children.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 15(3) → Women + Children

8. Article 15(4)

  • Article 15(4) enables special provisions for:
  • Socially and educationally backward classes.
  • Scheduled Castes.
  • Scheduled Tribes.
  • It was inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Amendment 1951 → Article 15(4)

9. Article 15(5)

  • Article 15(5) enables special provisions including reservation in admissions for SEBCs, SCs and STs.
  • It extends to specified private educational institutions, aided or unaided.
  • Minority educational institutions protected under Article 30(1) are excluded.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 15(5) → Educational Admissions + Specified Private Institutions

10. 93rd Constitutional Amendment

  • Article 15(5) was inserted through the 93rd Constitutional Amendment.
📌 Must-Memorise

93rd Amendment → Article 15(5)

11. Article 15(6)

  • Article 15(6) enables special provisions, including reservation, for Economically Weaker Sections outside the classes covered by Articles 15(4) and 15(5).
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 15(6) → EWS

12. 103rd Constitutional Amendment — 2019

  • The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 inserted:
  • Article 15(6).
  • Article 16(6).
  • It created the constitutional framework for EWS reservation.
📌 Must-Memorise

103rd Amendment → 2019 → EWS

13. Reservation in Educational Institutions

Reservation in education seeks to widen access to:

  • Professional courses.
  • Higher education.
  • Employment pathways.
  • Administrative representation.
  • Social mobility.

14. Central Educational Reservation Pattern

The supplied source identifies the broad Central reservation structure as:

  • SC → 15%.
  • ST → 7.5%.
  • OBC → 27%.
  • EWS → 10%.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Central Reservation Matrix ≠ Tamil Nadu State Matrix

15. Article 16(1)

  • Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity for citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to public office.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 16(1) → Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment

16. Article 16(4)

  • Article 16(4) permits reservation in appointments or posts for a backward class of citizens that, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in State services.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 16(4) → Backward Class + Inadequate Representation

17. Adequate Representation

  • The constitutional phrase is inadequate representation.
  • It does not mean every group's representation must exactly equal its population share.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Adequate Representation ≠ Exact Population Proportion

18. Reservation in Promotion

  • Reservation in initial appointment and reservation in promotion are constitutionally distinct issues.
  • Indra Sawhney held that Article 16(4), as interpreted in that case, did not itself authorise reservation in promotion.

19. 77th Constitutional Amendment — 1995

  • The 77th Amendment inserted Article 16(4A).
  • It concerns reservation in promotion for SCs and STs subject to constitutional requirements.
📌 Must-Memorise

77th Amendment → Article 16(4A) → Promotion

20. 81st Constitutional Amendment — 2000

  • The 81st Amendment inserted Article 16(4B).
  • It concerns carried-forward unfilled reserved vacancies treated as a separate class.
📌 Must-Memorise

81st Amendment → Article 16(4B) → Backlog Vacancies

21. 82nd Constitutional Amendment

  • The 82nd Amendment inserted a proviso to Article 335.
  • It permits specified relaxation in qualifying marks or evaluation standards for SC/ST promotion reservation under the constitutional framework.

22. 85th Constitutional Amendment — 2001

  • The 85th Amendment addressed consequential seniority in promotion for SC and ST employees within the applicable reservation framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

85th Amendment → Consequential Seniority

23. Article 16 Clause Memory Chain

  • Article 16(4) → Reservation in appointments/posts.
  • Article 16(4A) → Reservation in promotion for SC/ST.
  • Article 16(4B) → Backlog/carry-forward vacancies.

24. Article 330

  • Article 330 provides reservation of seats in the Lok Sabha for:
  • Scheduled Castes.
  • Scheduled Tribes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 330 → Lok Sabha → SC/ST

25. Article 332

  • Article 332 provides reservation of seats for SCs and STs in State Legislative Assemblies.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 332 → State Assemblies → SC/ST

26. Article 243D

  • Article 243D provides reservation in Panchayats.
  • It includes reservation for SCs, STs and women under the constitutional framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243D → Panchayats

27. Article 243T

  • Article 243T contains corresponding reservation provisions for Municipalities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243T → Municipalities

28. Women's Reservation — 106th Amendment

  • The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 inserted provisions for one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.
  • According to the supplied source, the relevant constitutional provisions commenced on 16 April 2026.

29. Women's Reservation — Operational Caution

  • According to the supplied source, Article 334A links actual implementation to delimitation after publication of figures from the first Census following the amendment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Constitutional Provision Exists ≠ Reservation Immediately Operational Before Required Delimitation

30. EWS Reservation

  • EWS reservation is based on economic weakness rather than the traditional social-and-educational backwardness framework.
  • The Constitution permits up to 10% reservation under Articles 15(6) and 16(6).
📌 Must-Memorise

EWS → 10% Constitutional Framework

31. Janhit Abhiyan Case — 2022

  • The constitutional validity of the 103rd Amendment was upheld by a majority of the Supreme Court Constitution Bench in:
  • Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, 2022.
📌 Must-Memorise

Janhit Abhiyan → 2022 → EWS Amendment Upheld

32. Central Medical AIQ Reservation

The supplied source records the Central All India Quota framework as:

  • SC → 15%.
  • ST → 7.5%.
  • OBC-NCL → 27%.
  • EWS → 10%.
  • PwD → Horizontal under applicable norms.

33. Tamil Nadu and EWS — Exam Caution

  • Students should not automatically add 10% EWS to Tamil Nadu's existing 69% communal-reservation matrix.
  • Tamil Nadu's published State matrix separately lists BC, BCM, MBC/DNC, SC and ST.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Central EWS Framework ≠ Automatic Addition to Tamil Nadu 69%

34. Article 340

  • Article 340 permits appointment of a commission to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 340 → Backward Classes Commission

35. Mandal Commission

  • The Second Backward Classes Commission was headed by B. P. Mandal.
  • Appointed → 1979.
  • Report → 1980.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mandal Commission → B. P. Mandal → 1979 / 1980

36. National Commission for Backward Classes

  • The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes.
📌 Must-Memorise

102nd Amendment → NCBC Constitutional Status

37. Articles 338B and 342A

  • Article 338B → National Commission for Backward Classes.
  • Article 342A → Socially and educationally backward classes under the constitutional framework.

38. 105th Constitutional Amendment — 2021

  • The 105th Amendment clarified the power of States and Union Territories to maintain their own lists of socially and educationally backward classes for their own purposes.
📌 Must-Memorise

105th Amendment → State SEBC Lists

39. Central List vs State List

  • Central OBC List and State BC/OBC Lists are not identical.
  • A community's classification for State purposes does not automatically create the same status under the Central List.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Central OBC List ≠ Tamil Nadu BC List

40. Vertical Reservation

Vertical reservation applies to major social categories such as:

  • SC.
  • ST.
  • OBC/BC.
  • MBC/DNC.
  • EWS under applicable frameworks.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vertical Reservation → Social/Community Category

41. Horizontal Reservation

Horizontal reservation cuts across vertical categories.

Examples may include:

  • Persons with benchmark disabilities.
  • Women where applicable.
  • Ex-servicemen.
  • Sports persons.
  • Government-school students under specified Tamil Nadu admission schemes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Horizontal Reservation → Cuts Across Vertical Categories

42. Vertical vs Horizontal Example

  • A candidate may belong vertically to SC.
  • If the candidate is also a person with benchmark disability, PwD operates horizontally under the applicable framework.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Vertical + Horizontal Can Apply to the Same Candidate

43. Open Competition — Meaning

  • Tamil Nadu's official framework treats Open Competition as open to candidates of all communities.
  • It is not exclusively reserved for forward-community candidates.
📌 Must-Memorise

OC = Open to Everyone

44. Reserved-Category Candidate Selected in OC

  • A meritorious BC, MBC/DNC, SC or ST candidate may be selected under Open Competition.
  • Such selection need not consume the candidate's reserved-category seat under applicable rules.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

OC ≠ Forward Community Quota

45. Tamil Nadu — 31% Open Competition

  • Under Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation framework:
  • Reserved categories → 69%.
  • Open Competition → 31%.
📌 Must-Memorise

69 Reserved + 31 Open = 100

46. Creamy Layer — Meaning

  • The creamy-layer principle excludes socially advanced sections within OBCs from specified reservation benefits under the Central OBC framework.
  • It became a major principle after Indra Sawhney.

47. Central OBC — Non-Creamy Layer

  • Central OBC reservation generally applies to OBC–Non-Creamy Layer under applicable Central criteria.
📌 Must-Memorise

Central OBC Reservation → OBC-NCL

48. Tamil Nadu and Creamy Layer

  • According to the supplied source, Tamil Nadu's State BC/MBC/DNC framework differs from the Central OBC-NCL system.
  • Tamil Nadu policy has opposed application of the Central creamy-layer exclusion to its State BC/MBC/DNC reservation structure.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Central OBC-NCL Rule ≠ Tamil Nadu BC/MBC Rule

49. Indra Sawhney Case — 1992

  • Indra Sawhney v. Union of India is popularly known as the Mandal Case.
  • It was decided by a nine-judge Bench in 1992.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indra Sawhney → 1992 → Mandal Case

50. Indra Sawhney — Major Principles

The judgment dealt with:

  • OBC reservation.
  • Creamy layer.
  • Reservation limits.
  • Backward-class classification.
  • Reservation in appointments.

51. 50% Rule

  • Indra Sawhney held that reservation under Article 16(4) should ordinarily not exceed 50%.
  • Exceptional circumstances were discussed, but 50% became the general constitutional norm.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indra Sawhney → General 50% Rule

52. Tamil Nadu — Historical Evolution

Tamil Nadu's reservation roots lie in:

  • Non-Brahmin Movement.
  • Justice Party.
  • Communal representation in Madras Presidency.
  • Post-Independence constitutional affirmative action.

53. Champakam Dorairajan — 1951

  • State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, 1951 challenged the communal allocation system.
  • It directly contributed to the First Constitutional Amendment and Article 15(4).
📌 Must-Memorise

Champakam → First Amendment → Article 15(4)

54. Tamil Nadu Reservation Reaches 69%

  • Tamil Nadu policy documents cited in the source record that the overall reservation level reached 69% in 1990.
  • The State thereafter maintained the 69% structure through legislation and constitutional protection measures.

55. Tamil Nadu — 69% Reservation Matrix

Current State communal reservation structure in the supplied source:

  • BC excluding BC Muslims → 26.5%.
  • BC Muslims → 3.5%.
  • MBC/DNC → 20%.
  • SC → 18%.
  • ST → 1%.
📌 Must-Memorise

26.5 + 3.5 + 20 + 18 + 1 = 69%

56. BC and BCM Split

  • Total BC allocation → 30%.
  • BC other than BCM → 26.5%.
  • Backward Class Muslims → 3.5%.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

BCM 3.5% Is Within the 30% BC Total

57. Backward Class Muslims — 3.5%

  • Tamil Nadu provides 3.5% reservation for Backward Class Muslims within the BC allocation.
  • The supplied source states that it has been implemented since 15 September 2007.
📌 Must-Memorise

BCM → 3.5% within BC Total

58. BCM — Eligibility Caution

  • The 3.5% allocation does not apply to all Muslims merely on the basis of religion.
  • It applies to Backward Class Muslims recognised under the State classification.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Religion Alone ≠ Automatic BCM Eligibility

59. Arunthathiyar Internal Reservation

  • Tamil Nadu provides an internal preferential reservation for Arunthathiyar communities within the Scheduled Caste quota.
  • The Tamil Nadu Arunthathiyars (Special Reservation) Act, 2009 created the statutory framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Arunthathiyar Act → 2009

60. SCA — 3% within SC 18%

The current matrix described in the source commonly separates:

  • SC → 15%.
  • SCA → 3%.

Combined:

15 + 3 = 18% SC total.

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

SCA 3% Is Within SC 18%

Not 18 + 3

61. Davinder Singh Case — 2024

  • In State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, 2024, a seven-judge Bench held that sub-classification within Scheduled Castes is constitutionally permissible subject to constitutional requirements.
  • The judgment discussed Tamil Nadu's Arunthathiyar framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Davinder Singh → 2024 → SC Sub-Classification Permissible in Principle

62. Tamil Nadu Reservation Act and 76th Amendment

  • Tamil Nadu enacted the Backward Classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Reservation Act.
  • It was published as Tamil Nadu Act 45 of 1994.
  • The 76th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1994 placed it in the Ninth Schedule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Act 45 of 1994

→ 76th Amendment

→ Ninth Schedule

63. Ninth Schedule Entry

  • The Tamil Nadu reservation law was placed in the Ninth Schedule as Entry 257A.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Reservation Law → Ninth Schedule Entry 257A

64. Ninth Schedule — Judicial Review Caution

  • Ninth Schedule placement does not provide absolute immunity from judicial review.
  • The supplied source refers to the I.R. Coelho basic-structure jurisprudence concerning post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule laws.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Ninth Schedule ≠ Total Immunity from Judicial Review

65. 7.5% Government-School Reservation

  • Tamil Nadu provides a special 7.5% preferential reservation for eligible government-school students in specified professional admissions.
  • It operates separately from the basic 69% vertical communal-reservation structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

7.5% Government-School Preference → Horizontal / Preferential

66. Medical and Engineering Admissions

According to the supplied source:

  • Medical admissions → 7.5% government-school reservation from 2020–21.
  • Engineering admissions → 7.5% for eligible students who studied Classes 6–12 in Tamil Nadu Government Schools under the applicable framework.

67. 69% and 7.5% — Do Not Add

  • 69% → Main vertical communal reservation.
  • 7.5% → Special horizontal/preferential reservation operating across applicable categories.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

69 + 7.5 ≠ 76.5% Independent Vertical Reservation

68. Vanniyar Internal Reservation — 2021

  • Tamil Nadu enacted legislation in 2021 providing 10.5% internal reservation for Vanniyars within the existing 20% MBC/DNC quota.
  • It was not intended as an additional quota beyond 20%.

69. Supreme Court Decision — 2022

  • The Madras High Court struck down the 10.5% internal reservation.
  • The Supreme Court upheld that outcome on 31 March 2022.
  • The supplied source states that the specific classification and quantum lacked adequate contemporaneous empirical data.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vanniyar 10.5% Case → 2022 → Data Justification Required

70. Internal Reservation — Constitutional Principle

  • Internal reservation is not automatically unconstitutional.
  • Classification and quantum require constitutional justification and reliable data.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sub-Classification → Permissible in Principle

But Requires Evidence + Constitutional Basis

  • Reservation is not merely a poverty-alleviation programme.
  • Article 14 → Equality before law and equal protection.
  • Article 15(3) → Women and children.
  • Article 15(4) → SEBCs, SCs and STs.
  • First Amendment 1951 → Article 15(4).
  • Article 15(5) → Educational admissions in specified institutions.
  • Article 15(6) → EWS.
  • 103rd Amendment 2019 → EWS.
  • Article 16(1) → Equality of opportunity in public employment.
  • Article 16(4) → Reservation for inadequately represented backward classes.
  • Article 16(4A) → Promotion for SC/ST.
  • Article 16(4B) → Backlog vacancies.
  • Article 330 → Lok Sabha SC/ST reservation.
  • Article 332 → State Assembly SC/ST reservation.
  • Article 243D → Panchayats.
  • Article 243T → Municipalities.
  • EWS and OBC reservation are different.
  • Central OBC quota → 27%.
  • Central OBC usually means OBC-NCL.
  • Central reservation matrix and Tamil Nadu matrix are different.
  • Mandal Commission → B. P. Mandal.
  • Mandal Commission appointed → 1979.
  • Report → 1980.
  • 102nd Amendment → NCBC constitutional status.
  • Article 338B → NCBC.
  • 105th Amendment → State SEBC-list power.
  • Vertical and horizontal reservation are different.
  • OC is open to all communities.
  • OC is not a forward-community quota.
  • Indra Sawhney → 1992.
  • Indra Sawhney → General 50% rule.
  • Tamil Nadu → 69% reservation.
  • Tamil Nadu OC → 31%.
  • BC → 26.5%.
  • BCM → 3.5%.
  • MBC/DNC → 20%.
  • SC → 18%.
  • ST → 1%.
  • BCM 3.5% is within BC 30%.
  • SCA 3% is within SC 18%.
  • Arunthathiyar Act → 2009.
  • Davinder Singh → 2024.
  • Tamil Nadu reservation law → Tamil Nadu Act 45 of 1994.
  • 76th Amendment → 1994.
  • Ninth Schedule Entry → 257A.
  • Ninth Schedule does not mean absolute judicial immunity.
  • 7.5% government-school reservation is not added vertically to 69%.
  • Vanniyar 10.5% was proposed within MBC/DNC 20%.
  • The 10.5% Vanniyar quota was struck down because the particular classification/quantum lacked adequate supporting data according to the supplied source.
  • Sub-classification can be constitutionally permissible when properly justified.
